title: Describing Data: The Task 1 Guide
subtitle: How to write clear, accurate Academic IELTS Task 1 reports on graphs, tables, charts, processes and maps
description: This guide shows you how to turn any Task 1 visual into a clear four-paragraph report. You will practise the overview, key features, and the language for graphs, tables, pie charts, processes and maps.
audience: Academic IELTS candidates at about Band 6 who want to reach Band 7 in Writing Task 1.

chapters.title: What Examiners Reward in Task 1
chapters.summary: Learn what Task 1 is, how it is marked, and the simple four-paragraph shape that most strong reports share.
chapters.body:
Writing Task 1 asks you to describe visual information. In Academic IELTS, this may be a line graph, bar chart, table, pie chart, process diagram or map. You must write at least 150 words. Most learners aim for about 170 to 190 words and spend around 20 minutes. Task 2 is longer and counts double, so Task 1 must not eat your time.

## The four criteria

Your report is marked on four equally weighted criteria.

- Task Achievement: did you cover the key features, give an overview and report the data accurately?
- Coherence and Cohesion: is the report organised into clear paragraphs with sensible linking?
- Lexical Resource: do you use varied and precise vocabulary for data?
- Grammatical Range and Accuracy: do you use a mix of sentence structures with few errors?

Notice that Task 1 uses the name Task Achievement. In Task 2 the first criterion is called Task Response. Both ask the same basic question: did you do what the task asked?

## What gets rewarded

Task 1 is a report, not an opinion essay. The examiner wants a clear and accurate picture of the information. In practice, strong reports usually show these habits.

- They paraphrase the title in the first sentence.
- They include a clear overview of the main pattern.
- They select key features instead of listing every number.
- They give accurate figures with units.
- They compare data, not just state it.
- They use a neutral, formal tone.

## What to avoid

Some habits cost marks again and again.

- Giving opinions or reasons. Do not write that numbers fell "because of load-shedding" unless the task tells you the reason.
- Copying the title word for word.
- Describing every single number.
- Forgetting units such as percent, millions or tonnes.
- Leaving out the overview.

## A simple structure

Use four paragraphs.

- Paragraph 1: introduction. One or two sentences that paraphrase the title.
- Paragraph 2: overview. Two or three sentences about the main trends or differences.
- Paragraph 3: first body paragraph with the first group of key features.
- Paragraph 4: second body paragraph with the second group.

Example: Imagine a task titled "The number of passengers using Dhaka Metro Rail, 2023 to 2025". Your introduction could be: "The line graph illustrates how many people travelled by Dhaka Metro Rail over a three-year period." Notice that "illustrates" replaces "shows", and "how many people travelled" replaces "the number of passengers using".

Tip: Divide your 20 minutes like this: about 3 minutes to study the task and plan, about 14 minutes to write, and about 3 minutes to check numbers, units and grammar. Practise this split until it feels natural.

## How this book works

Each chapter teaches one skill. First you will learn to write the overview. Then you will learn to choose key features. After that come the language for line graphs, bar charts and tables, and pie charts. The last chapter covers processes and maps and gives you a revision plan. All numbers in the examples are invented for practice, so do not treat them as real facts.

Read each chapter slowly. Write the exercise answer in your notebook. Short, regular practice will help you more than one long weekend of study.
takeaways: Task 1 needs at least 150 words and is a factual report, not an opinion.
Four equally weighted criteria are marked: Task Achievement, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy.
Use four paragraphs: introduction, overview, two body paragraphs.
Plan for about 20 minutes: plan, write, then check.
chapters.exercise: Write one sentence that paraphrases this title without copying it: "The percentage of households with internet access in four districts, 2020 to 2024." Then check that you changed at least three words or phrases.

chapters.title: Writing a Clear Overview
chapters.summary: Learn what an overview is, where to place it, and how to write one for every type of Task 1.
chapters.body:
The overview is the single most important paragraph in Task 1. It tells the examiner that you can see the big picture. A report with no clear overview often struggles to reach a higher band for Task Achievement, even if the details are correct.

## What an overview is

An overview is a short summary of the main pattern. It uses general words, not detailed numbers. It answers one question: if the reader saw only this paragraph, what would they understand about the information?

Put it in its own paragraph straight after the introduction. Start with a signal phrase so the examiner finds it quickly.

- Overall, ...
- In general, ...
- It is clear that ...
- The most striking feature is that ...

## Finding the main pattern

Ask yourself three questions.

- What is the biggest change, or the biggest difference?
- What is the highest and what is the lowest?
- Is there anything the groups have in common?

Your answers become your overview.

## Overviews for each task type

For a line graph, describe the general direction. For a bar chart, table or pie chart, describe the main comparison. For a process, say how many stages there are and what the start and end are. For a map, say what changed most.

Example: Suppose a line graph shows how Dhaka residents paid for shopping between 2018 and 2024. Cash fell and mobile payment rose. A strong overview would be: "Overall, mobile payment became much more popular, while the use of cash declined. Card payment remained the least common method throughout." There are no numbers, but the main story is clear.

Example: For a process showing how jute is turned into rope, you might write: "Overall, the process has six stages, beginning with harvesting the plants and ending with the production of rope."

## Two or three sentences is enough

You do not need a long paragraph. Two sentences that make two clear points are better than four vague ones. Choose the points that matter most.

## Common mistakes

- Putting numbers in the overview. Save numbers for the body.
- Writing an opinion, such as "This is a good change".
- Saying only "There are many changes". This says nothing.
- Writing the overview as a conclusion at the very end. Some examiners will still find it, but a separate paragraph near the top is safer.
- Describing one detail and ignoring the rest.

Tip: Write your overview first, before the body paragraphs. If you run out of time, you will already have the most valuable paragraph on the page.

## Checking your overview

Read it and ask: does it describe the whole graph, not just one line or one bar? Does it use general language? Could someone who has never seen the graph understand the main message?

If the answer to all three is yes, you are ready to write the body. If the graph has two clear groups, such as items that rose and items that fell, mention both groups in your overview. That small habit makes your report look complete and organised.
takeaways: The overview summarises the main pattern with no detailed numbers.
Place it in its own paragraph after the introduction.
Use signal phrases such as Overall or In general.
Write the overview first so it is never missed.
chapters.exercise: Look at any simple chart in a newspaper or textbook. Write a two-sentence overview that begins with "Overall," and contains no numbers.

chapters.title: Selecting Key Features
chapters.summary: Learn how to choose what to report and how to group data into two logical body paragraphs.
chapters.body:
Task 1 often shows far more data than you can describe in 170 to 190 words. You cannot report everything, and you should not try. Your job is to select the key features and organise them clearly.

## What counts as a key feature

Look for the points that a reader would notice first.

- The highest and lowest values
- The biggest increase or decrease
- A turning point, where a trend changes direction
- A crossover, where one line passes another
- A clear similarity between two groups
- An important exception

Minor ups and downs, small differences and tiny categories usually do not need their own sentence.

## A quick method

Spend two or three minutes on this routine before you write.

- Read the title, labels, units and time period.
- Underline or circle four to six key features.
- Decide the main pattern for your overview.
- Group your features into two sets for the body paragraphs.

## Grouping data

Good grouping gives your report logic. Do not describe each item in the order it appears. Instead, group items that share a pattern.

Example: Imagine a table showing the percentage of workers who use five ways to travel to work in Dhaka: bus, rickshaw, walking, car and motorbike. Suppose bus, rickshaw and walking are used by most people, while car and motorbike are used by few. Your first body paragraph could cover the three popular methods. Your second could cover the two less popular ones. This is clearer than five separate sentences in random order.

For a line graph, you might group lines that rose in one paragraph and lines that fell in another. For a bar chart with two years, you might compare the categories in the first year, then describe the changes.

## Using numbers wisely

Support each key feature with one or two figures. Do not add a number to every word. Always include the unit.

When the exact figure is hard to read, use approximation language.

- about, around, roughly
- just over, just under
- nearly, almost
- well over, well under

This is accurate and safe. Do not guess a precise figure that the graph does not show.

## Stay objective

Describe what you can see. Do not explain why. Do not predict unless the graph includes future data. A sentence such as "People stopped using rickshaws because of traffic" is not allowed, because the task does not give the reason.

Tip: After you choose your features, ask whether each one belongs in the overview or the body. Big, general patterns go in the overview. Specific figures go in the body.

## A balance check

Make sure both body paragraphs are roughly the same length. If one paragraph has eight sentences and the other has two, you have probably grouped badly. Move one or two features across.

Also check that no major feature is missing. Leaving out the highest value or the most obvious trend is a bigger error than leaving out a small detail.
takeaways: Select four to six key features instead of describing every number.
Look for highest, lowest, biggest change, turning points and crossovers.
Group features with similar patterns into two body paragraphs.
Use approximation words when exact values are unclear, and never explain reasons.
chapters.exercise: Choose a table or chart from a magazine. List five key features in note form, then split them into two groups and give each group a short label.

chapters.title: Line Graphs and Trend Language
chapters.summary: Build the verbs, adverbs and structures you need to describe change over time clearly and accurately.
chapters.body:
Line graphs show change over time, so your language must show direction, size and speed. The good news is that a small set of structures covers most graphs. Learn them well and use them accurately.

## Verbs for direction

- Upward: rise, increase, grow, climb, go up
- Downward: fall, decrease, decline, drop, go down
- No change: remain stable, stay constant, level off
- Highest point: reach a peak, peak at
- Lowest point: reach a low, hit a low, bottom out
- Up and down: fluctuate

## Describing size and speed

Add an adverb or adjective to show how big or how fast the change was.

- Big and fast: sharply, rapidly, dramatically
- Steady: steadily, gradually
- Small: slightly, marginally

Use these two patterns and vary them.

- Verb plus adverb: "The number of visitors rose sharply."
- There was a plus adjective plus noun: "There was a sharp rise in the number of visitors."

## Prepositions

Prepositions cause many errors, so learn them as fixed pairs.

- rose from 20 to 35: the start and end values
- rose by 15: the amount of change
- stood at 35: a value at one point
- reached a peak of 35: the highest value
- fluctuated between 20 and 30: the range

Example: Imagine a line graph of monthly electricity demand in a Dhaka neighbourhood from January to December, in megawatts. You could write: "Demand started at about 40 megawatts in January and then rose steadily to reach a peak of 75 megawatts in July. After that, it fell sharply to 50 megawatts by October."

## Time expressions

Link your sentences with time phrases so the reader can follow the story.

- between 2018 and 2022
- over the period
- by the end of the period
- in the following year
- after that, subsequently, thereafter

## Choosing the tense

Use the past simple for past years. Use the present perfect only if the period continues up to now. If the graph shows future years, use "is expected to" or "is predicted to". If there is no time, use the present simple.

Tip: Do not repeat "increase" five times. Use a small set of synonyms, but only words you are sure about. A simple word used correctly beats a difficult word used wrongly.

## Common errors

- "Rose to 15 percent" and "rose by 15 percent" mean different things. The first gives the final value. The second gives the size of the change.
- Forgetting the plural "s" after "the numbers".
- Saying "the graph increases". The graph does not increase. The data does.
- Using "fall down" when "fall" is enough.

## Describing two lines

When two lines cross or move in opposite directions, say so. For example: "Cash payments declined steadily, whereas mobile payments rose, overtaking cash in 2022." Showing the relationship between lines is exactly what the examiner wants to see.
takeaways: Learn verbs for rise, fall, stability, peak and fluctuation.
Add adverbs and adjectives to show size and speed.
Use prepositions correctly: from/to, by, at, between.
Use the past simple for past data, and mention crossovers between lines.
chapters.exercise: Write three sentences about an imaginary line graph of rice prices over five years. Use rose from/to, fell by, and reached a peak of.

chapters.title: Bar Charts and Tables: Making Comparisons
chapters.summary: Use comparative and superlative structures to compare categories, and organise bar charts and tables logically.
chapters.body:
Bar charts and tables are mainly about comparison. Where a line graph asks you to describe movement, these ask you to show how categories differ. That means your grammar must handle comparison well.

## Core comparison language

- Comparatives: higher than, lower than, more than, fewer than
- Superlatives: the highest, the lowest, the most popular, the least common
- Equality: the same as, similar to, as high as, almost identical
- Multiples: twice as high as, three times as many as, nearly double
- Contrast: whereas, while, in contrast, by comparison, on the other hand

Use "fewer" with countable nouns, such as fewer students. Use "less" with uncountable nouns, such as less rainfall.

## Comparing correctly

A common mistake is comparing things that are not the same type. Look at this sentence: "The price in Dhaka was higher than Sylhet." It compares a price with a city. Write instead: "The price in Dhaka was higher than that in Sylhet."

Another common mistake is doubling the comparison. Write "higher", not "more higher". Write "the highest", not "the most highest".

Example: Imagine a bar chart of the average monthly mobile data use, in gigabytes, of students in four age groups. You could write: "Students aged 18 to 20 used the most data, at about 14 gigabytes, which was nearly double the figure for those aged 24 to 26. In contrast, the oldest group used the least."

## Organising a bar chart

You have two main choices.

- By category: describe each group and how it changed.
- By time: compare all groups in the first year, then in the last year.

Pick the plan that gives you the clearest story and use it in both body paragraphs. For a chart with only one time period, rank the bars: first the highest, then the middle ones, then the lowest.

## Organising a table

A table has many numbers, so selection matters most. Scan each row and column to find the highest and lowest values. Then group similar rows. Do not read the table from left to right like a list.

Tip: Mix your sentence patterns. Begin some sentences with the subject, some with a time phrase, and some with a comparison. For example: "By 2024, rickshaws were used by fewer commuters than buses."

## Tense for tables

If the table has dates in the past, use the past simple. If it shows current information with no dates, use the present simple. If it covers past and future dates, switch carefully.

## Linking ideas

Use "whereas" and "while" inside one sentence to join two contrasting facts: "Buses carried 40 percent of commuters, whereas trains carried only 10 percent." Use "in contrast" at the start of a new sentence.

Do not overuse linkers. One linker per sentence is enough. Clear comparisons with correct grammar score better than long sentences full of connecting words.
takeaways: Bar charts and tables ask you to compare categories.
Use comparatives, superlatives, multiples and contrast words accurately.
Compare like with like: use that of or those of to avoid faulty comparisons.
Rank and group data instead of reading it as a list.
chapters.exercise: Write two sentences comparing two bars or two table cells of your choice. One must use whereas, and the other must use a multiple such as twice as or nearly double.

chapters.title: Pie Charts and Proportions
chapters.summary: Learn how to describe shares and percentages, and how to handle one pie or several.
chapters.body:
Pie charts show how a whole is divided. The total is usually 100 percent, so the key skill is describing proportions clearly and comparing them across categories or across years.

## Language for proportions

Use varied nouns and verbs so you do not repeat "percent" in every sentence.

- Nouns: proportion, percentage, share, figure, fraction
- Verbs: account for, make up, represent, constitute
- Adjectives: the largest, the smallest, the second largest

Example: "Natural gas accounted for the largest share of electricity generation, at 50 percent. Imported fuel made up a further 20 percent."

## Fractions and quantities

Fractions make your writing more natural and show lexical range. Learn these matches.

- 25 percent: a quarter, one in four
- 50 percent: a half
- 75 percent: three quarters
- 10 percent: one in ten
- About 33 percent: roughly a third
- Over 50 percent: the majority
- Under 10 percent: a small minority

Add approximation words for figures that are not exact: nearly a third, just over a quarter, well under a fifth.

## One pie chart

With one pie, rank the categories. Start with the biggest slice, then the second biggest. Group the small slices together at the end.

Example: Imagine a pie chart of how a Dhaka family spends its monthly budget. You might write: "Housing took up the biggest share of the budget, at about 40 percent, followed by food at a quarter. The remaining categories, including transport and education, each represented less than 15 percent."

Check that your numbers add up to about 100 percent. This stops you from mixing up a slice.

## Two or more pie charts

When there are two pies, such as two different years, do not describe each pie separately. That makes a list, not a comparison. Instead, describe what changed between them. Which slice grew? Which shrank? Which stayed almost the same?

Example: "The share of renewable energy rose from 10 percent to 25 percent, whereas the share of coal fell from 40 percent to 30 percent."

Tip: Use "percentage points" when you describe the difference between two percentages. If a share goes from 10 percent to 25 percent, it rose by 15 percentage points. This is more accurate than saying it rose by 15 percent.

## Pie charts with different totals

Sometimes the pies show different totals, such as the number of students in two years. A larger share in a smaller total may not mean a larger number. Mention the totals if the chart gives them, and compare shares carefully.

## Common errors

- Writing "the percentage of X is 20" without a verb phrase such as "accounted for".
- Forgetting the word "of": "a quarter of students", not "a quarter students".
- Using "people" and "peoples" incorrectly. Use "people" for the plural.
- Giving the same structure to every sentence.

Keep your introduction short, put the main comparison in your overview, and use the body paragraphs for the biggest and most interesting changes.
takeaways: Vary nouns and verbs such as share, proportion, account for and make up.
Learn fraction phrases: a quarter, a third, the majority, a small minority.
With several pies, describe the changes between them, not each pie in turn.
Use percentage points when you describe the difference between two percentages.
chapters.exercise: Write two sentences about a made-up pie chart of fruit sales. Use account for in one sentence and a fraction phrase in the other.

chapters.title: Processes, Maps and Your Revision Plan
chapters.summary: Describe processes and maps with sequence and location language, then follow a two-week plan to revise the whole book.
chapters.body:
Processes and maps look different from graphs, but the same rules apply. Write an introduction, an overview and two body paragraphs. Stay objective, and do not invent details that the diagram does not show.

## Describing a process

A process shows how something is made or how something happens. It may be a man-made process, such as making bricks, or a natural cycle, such as the life of a frog.

- Count the stages and note the start and end for your overview.
- Use the passive voice for most steps: "The clay is dug and then mixed with water."
- Use sequence words: first, next, then, after that, subsequently, finally.
- Use "once", "before" and "while" to join steps.

Example: "First, jute plants are harvested and soaked in water. Once the fibres have loosened, they are dried in the sun. Finally, the fibres are spun into rope."

For a cycle, say that there is no clear start or end. Choose one stage to begin with. Do not copy the labels word for word where you can use a natural alternative.

## Describing a map

Many map tasks show the same place at two times. Your overview should say what changed most, and also what stayed the same.

- Location: in the north, to the east of, next to, opposite, between
- Change: was replaced by, was converted into, was demolished, was built, was extended
- No change: remained unchanged, stayed the same

Use the past simple for the earlier map and the correct tense for the later map. If the later map shows the present or future, use the present simple or "will be".

Example: "A small village stood to the east of the river. Over time, the farmland was replaced by housing, and a new road was built to the south."

Tip: Describe the map systematically. Move from one side to the other, or group changes by type, such as new buildings and removed features. Never jump around.

## Your two-week revision plan

Short, focused practice works well. Aim for about 30 to 45 minutes a day, five days a week.

- Days 1 and 2: Rewrite ten titles as paraphrased introductions. Write five overviews with no numbers.
- Days 3 and 4: Take two charts and underline five key features. Group them and write a plan.
- Days 5 and 6: Practise trend language. Write one line graph report in 20 minutes.
- Days 7 and 8: Write one bar chart or table report and check your comparisons.
- Days 9 and 10: Write one pie chart report. Practise fractions and percentage points.
- Days 11 and 12: Write one process and one map report. Check passive verbs and location words.
- Days 13 and 14: Do two timed full reports. Check the 150-word minimum, overview, units and grammar. Make a list of your three most common errors.

Keep every report in one folder. After two weeks, read the first one and the last one. The difference is your progress.
takeaways: For processes, use sequence words and the passive voice.
For maps, use location words and change verbs, and describe changes systematically.
Always write an overview, even for processes and maps.
Follow a two-week plan and keep a list of your repeated errors.
chapters.exercise: Choose one process or map from a textbook. Write the overview in two sentences, then list five sequence or location phrases you could use in the body.
